units.source_excerpt: In this paper, we formulate an excess water ratio (EWR) metric for water scarcity that improves upon currently used metrics
units.function: Open with the new indicator and its relationship to an established benchmark.

features.clause_structure: main action plus benchmark relative clause

units.reusable_pattern: We formulate {new indicator} for {problem}, extending {benchmark} by {missing dimension}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim improvement before naming the added information.

units.source_excerpt: we start with the amount of naturally available water, then subtract out water usage from each primary category
units.function: Compress the balance mechanism into an ordered operation.
units.reusable_pattern: Start with {resource supply}, subtract {use categories}, and normalize by {exposure unit}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not hide omitted balance terms.

units.source_excerpt: In our case study, we apply our model to India
units.function: Name the case and immediately attach decision-relevant reasons.
units.reusable_pattern: Apply {model} to {case}, where {scale} and {harm} make the decision urgent.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not select a case only because data are convenient.

units.source_excerpt: We develop a secondary model on MATLAB that utilizes local predictions of water use and population growth from the Indian government
units.function: Distinguish a second forecast model by data authority and computational role.

features.clause_structure: model action plus source relative clause

units.reusable_pattern: Develop a second {model} using {local authority projections} to extrapolate {decision indicator}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call two models mutually validating without reconciliation.

units.source_excerpt: Taking these two models together, we conclude that the excess water per capita in India will be around half of its current level by 2031.
units.function: Synthesize two forecast branches into one timed headline result.
units.reusable_pattern: Across {models}, {indicator} is projected to {magnitude} by {horizon}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not merge conflicting model outputs without explaining the synthesis rule.

units.source_excerpt: We proceed to explore several intervention measures for India's water crisis that emphasize the need to address the supply and demand sides
units.function: Organize interventions by the two sides of the resource balance.
units.reusable_pattern: Evaluate {interventions} on both the {supply} and {demand} sides of {balance}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not compare policies on one side while claiming a balanced portfolio.

units.source_excerpt: large cultural shifts in demand for water will ultimately be necessary for India to achieve long-term water sustainability
units.function: Close by translating scenario comparison into a strategic demand-side conclusion.
units.reusable_pattern: Because {supply measures} shift {outcome} only modestly, long-run success requires {demand change}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not turn one stylized scenario into universal necessity.

units.source_excerpt: Every human needs at a bare minimum 20 liters of water to survive.
units.function: Anchor global stakes in a biological threshold before discussing aggregate demand.
units.reusable_pattern: Begin with {minimum human requirement} and its {consequences}, then name the first demand category.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use dramatic biology without a source and analytical handoff.

units.source_excerpt: personal use is actually a fairly small - if absolutely essential - piece of the pie
units.function: Correct the opening intuition by partitioning total use across sectors.
units.reusable_pattern: Although {use} is essential, it represents {share}; {dominant sector} accounts for {larger share}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not let moral importance substitute for system share.

units.source_excerpt: The problem arises when we consider the conditions that make water usable: it must be fresh, liquid, and physically accessible.
units.function: Resolve the apparent abundance paradox through successive usability filters.
units.reusable_pattern: Resolve {abundance paradox} by applying {quality}, {state}, and {access} filters.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not equate total stock with usable supply.

units.source_excerpt: The main reason to expect that condition to be different going forward is that the exponential nature of human population growth
units.function: Move from historical replenishment to a forward demand stressor with a compressed timeline.
units.reusable_pattern: Although {system} sustained past demand, {driver} changes the forward trajectory, as shown by {timeline}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not infer exponential continuation without a stated forecast source.

units.source_excerpt: This ongoing massive increase in the number of people around the world drives up water usage in all three categories.
units.function: Propagate the population driver through personal, industrial, agricultural, and pollution pathways.

features.clause_structure: main causal claim plus repeated it means clauses

units.reusable_pattern: {Driver} raises {direct use}, expands {economic use}, increases {food use}, and reduces usable supply through {externality}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not double count a driver in later sector equations.

units.source_excerpt: modeling future water needs and developing strategies we are all able and willing to implement
units.function: Close the background by pairing forecast accuracy with implementable intervention design.
units.reusable_pattern: The task is to model {future need} and design {implementable action} within {physical limit}.
prohibited_generalizations: Avoid apocalyptic language that outruns the modeled scope.

units.source_excerpt: we start with a reflection of the Water Stress Indicator (WSI)
units.function: Begin model design from an established indicator rather than an isolated invention.
units.reusable_pattern: Start from {established indicator}, state its {authority/use}, and reproduce its definition.
prohibited_generalizations: Authority use is not evidence that the indicator fits every decision.

units.source_excerpt: Water withdrawals are thus interpreted as a reflection of water use and the MAR is interpreted as a reflection of water availability.
units.function: Assign semantic roles to numerator and denominator before modification.
units.reusable_pattern: Interpret {numerator} as {pressure} and {denominator} as {capacity} before changing the ratio.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat a proxy component as direct measurement without qualification.

units.source_excerpt: A significant weakness with the use of the WSI is that it does not allow for any conclusions to be drawn about the average impact of water scarcity on an individual level.
units.function: Name one missing decision scale and explain it with a population contrast.
units.reusable_pattern: {Benchmark} cannot answer {decision-scale question}; equal {aggregate states} can imply different {unit impacts}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not invent a new metric without a specific unresolved question.

units.source_excerpt: formulating a ratio that determines how much water this leaves per capita for recreational, commercial, or hygienic uses
units.function: Translate the benchmark gap into a concrete output and use interpretation.
units.reusable_pattern: Define {new estimand} as {balance} per {unit}, interpreted for {remaining uses}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not imply water quality or spatial access from a national volume balance.

units.source_excerpt: Because it is impossible to account for the impact of each of these factors on the overall water demands and availability, we adopt a number of simplifying assumptions

units.reusable_pattern: Because {factor set} cannot all be represented in {target model}, adopt {bounded assumptions}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use complexity as the only justification for consequential omissions.

units.source_excerpt: The only source of water for a region is its MAR.

units.reusable_pattern: Assume {dominant source} is the modeled supply because {precedent}; exclude {alternatives} over {scope}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call excluded transfers or storage physically nonexistent.

units.source_excerpt: Utility from water use for individuals is a strictly increasing monotonic function.
units.function: Connect a mathematical monotonicity assumption to cross-cultural interpretation.
units.reusable_pattern: Assume {utility} is {monotonic property}, implying {directional consequence} across {heterogeneity}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not infer equal marginal benefit across populations.

units.source_excerpt: The current aggregate level of water use is in a temporary equilibrium
units.function: Define a current-state constraint and its contradiction-based justification.

features.quantitative_role: use less than or equal to supply

units.reusable_pattern: Treat {current aggregate} as a temporary equilibrium under {capacity}, since the opposite would imply {contradiction}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not let an equilibrium assumption erase groundwater stock depletion or imports.

units.source_excerpt: we do not consider the effect of transportation of water in our model
units.function: State a geographic omission and explain the aggregation consequence.
units.reusable_pattern: Exclude {spatial process}; therefore interpret {output} only at {aggregate scale}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not apply national averages to local access decisions.

units.source_excerpt: the difference between Water Use and Water Availability
units.function: Introduce the central balance in words before its formula.
units.reusable_pattern: Define {surplus/deficit} as {availability} minus {use} before displaying the equation.
prohibited_generalizations: Keep sign convention consistent across all later equations.

units.source_excerpt: A higher ratio implies that there is a greater amount of water available for the region
units.function: Interpret indicator direction immediately after definition.
units.reusable_pattern: Higher {indicator} means {physical quantity} per {unit}, hence {decision interpretation}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not infer safety, timing, or distribution from volume alone.

units.source_excerpt: our model needs to account for the water factors that impact the region over time
units.function: Expand the indicator into forecastable sector and driver components.
units.reusable_pattern: To forecast {indicator}, decompose {balance terms} into {output}, {footprint}, {population}, and {climate} drivers.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not multiply growth rates without checking units and base definitions.

units.source_excerpt: we can introduce a variable that represents the amount of water imported or exported from a region
units.function: Repair omitted balance channels by adding imports and environmental requirements.
units.reusable_pattern: Extend {base balance} with {transfer term} and {environmental reserve} when the decision requires them.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not reverse the original surplus sign when extending the model.

units.source_excerpt: We must begin with an accurate interpretation of India's water stress to determine how its current level of water usage will impact the future.
units.function: Require a baseline reconstruction before projecting change.
units.reusable_pattern: Before forecasting, reconstruct {current indicator} from {dated inputs} and verify its interpretation.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not mix source years without disclosure.

units.source_excerpt: We use this summation to tell fully account for all the growth factors that affect water use.
units.function: Combine sector-specific growth equations into one total-use forecast.
units.reusable_pattern: Model each {sector} from its own drivers, then sum them into {total demand}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not apply one growth rate to heterogeneous components without support.

units.source_excerpt: The final will become negative at some point before water availability.
units.function: Translate sector projections into a shortage crossing and human consequence.
units.reusable_pattern: Combine {projected components}; compare with {capacity}; report when {balance} crosses {threshold}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not hide conflict with an alternate forecast horizon.

units.source_excerpt: we can utilize a polynomial regression to fit the data points using MATLAB's polyfit function
units.function: State the sparse-knot interpolation method and its computational tool.
units.reusable_pattern: Fit {category projections} at {dated knots} with {interpolator}, then combine them into {indicator}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not extrapolate far beyond the last knot without degree and uncertainty diagnostics.

units.source_excerpt: By incorporating the components provided in the Water & Water Related Statistics report, the excess water ratio can be evaluated as follows

units.reusable_pattern: Using {official category table}, expand {aggregate term} into {named components} before scenario changes.
prohibited_generalizations: Keep the source definition and sign convention unchanged.

units.source_excerpt: These projections of water use have serious direct impacts to the persons of India and to their ability to satisfy basic needs.
units.function: Move from national indicator trajectories to citizen-level channels.
units.reusable_pattern: Translate {national trajectory} into {household}, {economic}, and {health} consequences.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not infer distributional harm from a national average without qualification.

units.source_excerpt: The relationship between the WSI and the EWR can be easily and accurately compared
units.function: Introduce a benchmark comparison with aligned country inputs.
units.reusable_pattern: Compare {new indicator} with {benchmark} on {same units/cases}, then display both values.
prohibited_generalizations: Algebraic correlation is not independent validation.

units.source_excerpt: As WSI increases, EWR decreases
units.function: State the observed direction before offering causal interpretation.
units.reusable_pattern: As {benchmark} rises, {new indicator} falls; explain the shared algebra and added {dimension}.

units.source_excerpt: The most pertinent statistic in water scarcity is how much excess water there is per person
units.function: Tie the indicator's strength to its intended decision scale.
units.reusable_pattern: A strength is {feature}: it exposes {decision-scale quantity} hidden by {aggregate benchmark}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not assert relevance for decisions the metric does not encode.

units.source_excerpt: the model should be applied to a region of any size to determine the overall water scarcity in the area
units.function: Bound model availability to scale and data access.
units.reusable_pattern: A limitation is {missing data/process}; use the model only at {supported scale}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not state a weakness without its effect on use.

units.source_excerpt: By aggregating water use across the region, we are unable to distinguish water use based on locality and seasonality.
units.function: Name the exact information lost through aggregation.
units.reusable_pattern: By {aggregation}, the model loses {spatial detail} and {temporal detail}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not describe aggregation as harmless simplification.

units.source_excerpt: we chose India as the country for our case study

units.reusable_pattern: Choose {case} because {scale}, {access deficit}, {health burden}, and {resource condition} jointly stress the model.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not rely on one headline statistic for case selection.

units.source_excerpt: India's water scarcity is seasonal and spatial variability in the rainfall.
units.function: Start the driver diagnosis with hydrologic variability and infrastructure response.
units.reusable_pattern: Identify {physical variability}, then trace how {infrastructure response} amplifies {stock pressure}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat infrastructure only as a solution when it changes stocks.

units.source_excerpt: This results in low quality infrastructure, which requires stakeholders to raise their taxes
units.function: Connect governance finance to service quality and distributional conflict.
units.reusable_pattern: Low {investment} weakens {infrastructure}, shifting {cost} toward {stakeholders} and intensifying {conflict}.

units.source_excerpt: Agricultural water use in India is largely dominated by the production of water-intensive crops
units.function: Name the dominant demand sector and connect crop choice to future pressure.
units.reusable_pattern: {Sector} dominates demand because {activity}; {growth driver} will expand it unless {practice} changes.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not recommend crop change without adoption constraints.

units.source_excerpt: the availability of water is being reduced through water pollution

units.reusable_pattern: Scarcity reflects not only {quantity pressure} but also {quality loss} and {access deficit}.

units.source_excerpt: the most comprehensive water scarcity interventions address both the demand and supply sides

units.reusable_pattern: Following {authority}, organize interventions into {supply} and {demand} branches and state exclusions.

units.source_excerpt: a 2005 study that performed a meta-analysis of 311 watershed development case studies

units.source_excerpt: On average then, each project has provided irrigation needed for 684 hectares.

units.reusable_pattern: Convert {case totals} to {per-project effect}, multiply by {unit intensity}, then size {portfolio}.

units.source_excerpt: We assume in our model that these watersheds will begin construction in the next year

units.reusable_pattern: Assume {intervention} starts in {year}, follows {reference duration}, and affects the model from {activation year}.

units.source_excerpt: While pricing information for waste treatment plants is not readily available, the construction would be very expensive.

units.source_excerpt: For the purposes of constructing our model to predict future water availability, we do not assume that this change will be enacted or successful.

units.reusable_pattern: Discuss {policy} as decision context but state that it is not included in {quantified forecast}.

units.source_excerpt: we have considered the water impact of switching all of India's wheat and rice production to millet over the course of 30 years

units.reusable_pattern: Model {baseline activities} switching to {alternative} over {horizon}; compute savings per {unit}.

units.source_excerpt: there is no evidence of negative impacts on the surrounding areas

units.source_excerpt: the use of treated water may alter soil quality over time

units.source_excerpt: This poses a health risk to communities that are located downstream of the area

units.source_excerpt: identifies many social and economic benefits of watershed development
